BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the result first (what it makes). 2) inputs and the place. 3) each step with its cause and its condition. 4) what breaks when a step fails. 5) the whole run once more at speed. 6) recap as a flow.
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the whole in context. 2) zoom into each part in a fixed path (outside to inside). 3) function of each part tied to its shape. 4) how the parts work together. 5) labelled recap.
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the basis of division first. 2) the tree from the top down. 3) each kind with its identifying feature and an example. 4) the borderline cases and exceptions. 5) the tree as recap.
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
  Teaching pattern: 1) what is common. 2) criteria one at a time, both sides together. 3) the reason behind each difference. 4) the most confused pair named directly. 5) difference table as recap.
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the period and its atmosphere. 2) events in order with their causes. 3) the people and their choices. 4) the turning point. 5) what changed after. 6) timeline recap.
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the effect students can see. 2) the cause. 3) each link of the chain with its mechanism. 4) the evidence. 5) the exception or limit. 6) the chain as recap.
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the fact in one line. 2) the number shown to scale against something familiar. 3) where it comes from (book or outside, dated). 4) what it changes or proves. 5) a formula built term by term when there is one.
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) what the figure is and why it is here. 2) a reading path across it (labels in order). 3) the one thing to remember from it. 4) link back to the text it explains.
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) a concrete example first. 2) the book's definition word by word. 3) a non-example that tests the boundary. 4) where the term is used next in the chapter.

Video v10: Plant की बाहरी covering और gas exchange
Goal: तुम epidermis और cuticle का protective role तथा stomata और guard cells का फर्क समझकर दोनों practice questions हल करोगे।
Opening hook: Leaf की covering protection भी दे और gases को आने-जाने भी दे—यह कैसे होगा?
Story or analogy: (none)
Planned minutes: 4
Narration time (S2-01): 3.2-4.2 minutes, about 416-546 spoken words (BIE counts 130 words a minute)
Prerequisites already taught in the prerequisite video (remind of one in at most 2 beats): Cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and basic plant-cell parts; Chromosome sets, DNA copying and nuclear versus cell division; Body covering, cavity, lumen and gland duct; Diffusion, absorption and secretion; Strength, flexibility, elasticity and rigidity; Contraction, relaxation, fatigue and voluntary control; Root and shoot tips, nodes, internodes, leaf base and girth; Photosynthesis, food storage and root water–mineral uptake

Items (item id | page | kind | type | content), each with its teacher questions (question id | ask | question → answer | basis):
p014-i5 | 14 | question | none | Q. …………… layer is thickest and helps in protection against water loss and further secrete a waxy substance on outer surface:
  p014-i5#q1 | what | What properties does the question ask the learner to associate with a layer? → The stem describes the layer as 'thickest', protective against water loss and secreting a waxy substance on the outer surface. | book
  p014-i5#q2 | which | Which option is the intended answer? → Option b, Epidermis, is the intended answer because the protective surface and waxy-covering clues point to the epidermis. | outside
  p014-i5#q3 | where | Where is the epidermis situated? → It forms the outer covering of the primary plant body, including leaves and young stems. | outside
  p014-i5#q4 | how | How does the waxy outer covering reduce water loss? → Epidermal cells of aerial plant parts secrete material forming a cuticle. Its water-resistant character reduces evaporation through the exposed surface. | outside
  p014-i5#q5 | why | Why should 'thickest' not be memorised as a general property of epidermis? → Epidermis is commonly a single cell layer. Its thickness and the thickness of its cuticle vary, and the stem gives no comparison that establishes it as the thickest layer. | outside
p014-i6 | 14 | answer_option | none | a. Sclerenchyma
  p014-i6#q1 | what | What is sclerenchyma? → It is a supporting plant tissue whose mature cells generally have thick, lignified walls and are dead. | outside
  p014-i6#q2 | why | Why is it a plausible distractor but not the intended answer? → Its thick walls may attract a learner focusing on 'thickest', but its main role is mechanical support. The wax-secreting protective surface described in the question points to epidermis. | outside
p014-i7 | 14 | answer_option | none | b. Epidermis
  p014-i7#q1 | what | What is epidermis in a plant? → It is the outer protective tissue covering the primary plant body. | outside
  p014-i7#q2 | how | How does its position help explain its protective function? → As the tissue at the exposed surface, it separates underlying tissues from the surroundings. In aerial parts its cuticle helps restrict surface water loss. | outside
  p014-i7#q3 | why | Why is this the intended answer despite the wording problem? → The combination of an outer protective layer and a secreted waxy covering identifies epidermis more closely than the other options; 'thickest' remains an imprecise clue. | outside
p014-i8 | 14 | answer_option | none | c. Parenchyma
  p014-i8#q1 | what | What is parenchyma? → It is a simple permanent plant tissue of living cells, generally with relatively thin cell walls, serving functions such as storage. | outside
  p014-i8#q2 | why | Why does parenchyma not fit the specific clues in the stem? → The stem asks for the external protective layer associated with a waxy surface covering. That description identifies epidermis rather than general storage or ground parenchyma. | outside
p014-i9 | 14 | answer_option | none | d. Suberin
  p014-i9#q1 | what | What is suberin? → Suberin is a water-resistant substance deposited in certain plant cell walls, notably those of cork cells. | outside
  p014-i9#q2 | why | Why is suberin a tempting but unsuitable answer here? → Its association with limiting water movement matches part of the clue, but suberin is a substance rather than the named tissue layer sought by the question. Epidermis is the intended option. | outside
  p014-i9#q3 | difference | How does the suberin association differ from the epidermal cuticle association? → Suberin is associated with walls such as those of cork cells. The epidermis of aerial parts commonly bears a cuticle containing cutin and waxes on its outer surface. | outside
p014-i10 | 14 | question | none | Q. Site of gaseous exchange on leaf is:
  p014-i10#q1 | what | What relationship does this question test? → It asks the learner to identify the site of gaseous exchange on a leaf from four listed structures or tissues. | book
  p014-i10#q2 | which | Which option answers the question? → Option b, Stomata, is the correct textbook answer. | outside
  p014-i10#q3 | how | How do stomata permit gaseous exchange? → Their pores connect the atmosphere with internal leaf air spaces. Gases diffuse through these openings according to concentration differences. | outside
  p014-i10#q4 | why | Why should guard cells be distinguished from the site itself? → Guard cells regulate the opening and closing of the stomatal pore; the pore provides the passage through which gases move. | outside
p014-i11 | 14 | answer_option | none | a. Guard cells
  p014-i11#q1 | what | What are guard cells? → They are specialised epidermal cells surrounding a stomatal pore. | outside
  p014-i11#q2 | how | How do guard cells influence gas exchange? → Changes in their turgor alter the pore opening, regulating gas movement and water-vapour loss. They control the passage rather than being the passage itself. | outside
p014-i12 | 14 | answer_option | none | b. Stomata
  p014-i12#q1 | what | What are stomata? → They are pores in the epidermis, each associated with guard cells, that provide routes for leaf gas exchange. | outside
  p014-i12#q2 | how | How are gas exchange and water loss linked at stomata? → An open pore allows carbon dioxide and oxygen to diffuse between the leaf and the atmosphere, while water vapour can also diffuse outward. Guard-cell regulation therefore affects both gas exchange and transpiration. | outside
p014-i13 | 14 | answer_option | none | c. Aerenchyma
  p014-i13#q1 | what | What is aerenchyma? → It is parenchyma with conspicuous air spaces, common in aquatic plants, where it aids internal aeration and buoyancy. | outside
  p014-i13#q2 | why | Why is an air-space tissue not the answer to this leaf-surface question? → Internal air spaces help gases move within plant organs, but the question asks for the site of exchange on the leaf surface, which is identified as stomata. | outside
p014-i14 | 14 | answer_option | none | d. Chlorenchyma
  p014-i14#q1 | what | What is chlorenchyma? → It is parenchyma containing chloroplasts and specialised for photosynthesis. | outside
  p014-i14#q2 | why | Why is chlorenchyma not the best answer even though photosynthesis uses gases? → Photosynthetic tissue uses carbon dioxide, but the surface openings through which gases pass are stomata. Gas use inside a tissue and exchange through a surface opening are distinct functions. | outside

output.title: Plant की covering: protection और gas exchange

frame.process: Epidermis protects the primary plant body; its aerial cuticle restricts surface water loss.
frame.how: Explain the exposed covering and water-resistant cuticle, then distinguish the four options.
frame.when: Teach the protective relationship before answering the first question.
frame.conditions: Cuticle and epidermal thickness vary; 'thickest' is not a reliable general property.
frame.atmosphere: Picture a leaf or young stem exposed to surrounding air.

frame.process: Stomatal pores permit leaf gas exchange, while guard cells regulate their opening.
frame.how: Connect outside air to internal leaf spaces through pores and distinguish passage, controller and internal tissues.
frame.when: Explain exchange before solving the second question; opening permits both gas movement and water-vapour loss.
frame.conditions: Diffusion depends on concentration differences; guard-cell turgor alters pore opening.
frame.atmosphere: Picture the leaf epidermis separating internal air spaces from the atmosphere.

beats.say: Leaf की covering पानी का loss कम भी करे और gases को आने-जाने भी दे—दोनों कैसे होंगे? आज 2 questions से समझो: protection कौन देता है, passage कौन बनाता है, और उसे control कौन करता है।
beats.on_screen: Leaf outline: water loss protection / gas exchange

beats.say: पहले concept समझो। Epidermis primary plant body की बाहरी protective covering है; leaves और young stems पर भी मिलती है। बाहर होने से यह अंदर के tissues को surroundings से अलग रखती है।
beats.on_screen: Leaf cross-section: outer Epidermis; underlying tissues

beats.say: हवा के संपर्क वाले plant parts की epidermal cells बाहर cuticle बनाने वाला material secrete करती हैं। Cuticle में cutin और waxes होते हैं। यह water-resistant covering बाहर से evaporation कम करती है; epidermis tissue है, cuticle उसके बाहर की covering।
beats.on_screen: Outside → cuticle containing cutin and waxes → epidermis

beats.say: अब question में layer को 'thickest' कहा है, जो water loss से बचाती है और बाहर waxy substance secrete करती है। Protective covering और wax वाले clues से intended answer b, Epidermis है। लेकिन 'thickest' मत याद करना: epidermis आम तौर पर single cell layer है; उसकी और cuticle की thickness बदल सकती है।
beats.on_screen: b. Epidermis ✓ | 'thickest': unreliable generalisation

beats.say: Sclerenchyma की mature cells आम तौर पर dead, thick और lignified walls वाली होती हैं; मुख्य काम mechanical support है, waxy covering बनाना नहीं। Parenchyma living, relatively thin-walled cells वाला simple permanent tissue है, जो storage जैसे काम करता है। इसलिए c भी इस protective covering का answer नहीं।
beats.on_screen: a. Sclerenchyma: support ✗ | c. Parenchyma: storage ✗

beats.say: Suberin water-resistant substance है, खासकर cork cells की walls में मिलता है। Water loss वाला clue इसे tempting बनाता है, लेकिन question tissue layer पूछता है, substance नहीं। Cork walls का suberin और epidermis के बाहर cutin तथा waxes वाली cuticle अलग associations हैं।
beats.on_screen: Suberin → cork cell walls | Cuticle → outside epidermis

beats.say: अब leaf में gas exchange का रास्ता देखो। Stomata epidermis के pores हैं, जो बाहर की हवा को अंदर के air spaces से जोड़ते हैं। Concentration differences के कारण carbon dioxide और oxygen इनके रास्ते diffuse करती हैं; खुले pore से water vapour भी बाहर जा सकती है।
beats.on_screen: Stomatal pore: atmosphere ↔ internal air spaces; water vapour outward

beats.say: Guard cells pore के आसपास की specialised epidermal cells हैं। उनके turgor, यानी पानी के कारण अंदर के pressure में बदलाव, pore का खुलना बदलते हैं। इसलिए वे gas movement और transpiration को regulate करती हैं: passage stomatal pore है, controller guard cells हैं।
beats.on_screen: Label pore separately from surrounding Guard cells

beats.say: Question है: leaf पर gaseous exchange का site कौन-सा है? Answer b, Stomata; a, Guard cells नहीं। पहचानो कि पूछा passage है, उसका control नहीं।
beats.on_screen: Site of gaseous exchange: b. Stomata ✓

beats.say: Aerenchyma बड़े air spaces वाला parenchyma है, aquatic plants में internal aeration और तैरने में मदद करता है। अंदर gases की movement में मदद करना और leaf पर exchange का opening होना अलग बातें हैं। इसलिए c नहीं।
beats.on_screen: Aerenchyma: internal air spaces ≠ surface pore

beats.say: Chlorenchyma chloroplasts वाला parenchyma है, जो photosynthesis करता है। Carbon dioxide इस्तेमाल करने वाला tissue और उसके आने-जाने का opening अलग हैं, इसलिए d नहीं। याद रखो: protection में Epidermis, gas passage में Stomata, control में Guard cells।
beats.on_screen: Chlorenchyma: photosynthesis | Epidermis protects; Stomata provide passage; Guard cells regulate

problems.problem: The maker's note claims 'approximately 530 spoken words', whereas the actual spoken word count across b1–b11 is around 375–385 words.
problems.fix: Update the word count note if regenerated; for a 1-page practice-question unit (10 short MCQ items), ~380 words (~3 minutes) is concise and covers every single question without artificial padding.

All item IDs (p014-i5 to p014-i14) and all 24 teacher questions are genuinely answered in the beats that claim them.
